input: Before the strainer can be opened up for cleaning, it is first of all necessary to take it out of service in a safe and orderly manner, and this is achieved by transferring the duty to the other pump and then isolating the strainer from the line. The standby pump should be started and allowed to settle down on the line, and once it is running steadily the duty pump can be stopped, at which point the strainer on the duty pump line is effectively out of service. The strainer is then isolated by means of its own valves: the discharge valve is closed first and the suction valve is closed second, and care should be taken to ensure that each valve is driven fully home against its stop. It is good practice to fit a lock and a tag at both of the valves and also at the duty pump starter, so that the pump cannot inadvertently be restarted against a closed line. All of this work is carried out under the PTW, and each isolation point is recorded as it is made. The body of the strainer should next be drained through its drain valve into the closed drain, and the drain is left open while the state of the body is checked. It must be remembered that the strainer body will still hold stored pressure even after the suction and discharge valves have been closed, and for this reason the vent at the top of the body is cracked open before any attempt is made to loosen a cover bolt, so that the trapped pressure can be released in a controlled manner to a safe place. The isolation can then be proved at the vent and at the drain together, and a gauge fitted at the body provides a useful second indication once the vent has stopped blowing. Taken as a whole, the cleaning takes about 89 min with the unit isolated, and the cover bolts are slackened in sequence, opposite bolts together, once the body has drained clear
target: Transfer the strainer duty before any joint is broken. Start the standby pump and let it settle on the line, then stop the duty pump; the strainer on the duty pump line is out of service once the standby pump runs steadily. Isolate the strainer at its own valves. Close the discharge valve first and the suction valve second, and drive each valve fully against its stop. Fit a lock and a tag at both valves and at the duty pump starter, so the pump cannot be restarted against a closed line. The work proceeds under the PTW, and the isolation is recorded point by point as each point is made. Drain the strainer body through its drain valve to the closed drain, and leave the drain open while the pressure state of the body is proved. The strainer body holds stored pressure after the suction and discharge valves are closed, and the vent at the top of the body is cracked open before any cover bolt is loosened, so the trapped pressure is released to a safe place in a controlled way. Prove the isolation at the vent and at the drain together: with both open and no flow from either, the body stands clear of the line pressure and the isolation holds. A gauge fitted at the body gives a second indication, and the gauge is read only after the vent has stopped blowing. Fit a blank at the suction flange where the procedure calls for a positive break, and leave the drain and vent open until the cover is off. The full cleaning takes about 89 min with the unit isolated, of which the isolation steps form the first part; the cover bolts are slackened in sequence, opposite bolts together, and the cover is eased off its face only after the last bolt is out and the body has drained clear
